system: You rewrite research decisions as topic-neutral abstractions. Return only the JSON object asked for.
prompt:
Below are research decisions made by several different researchers. Rewrite each one into the fixed
template below so that a reader cannot tell what field, topic, paper, organisation or person it comes from, nor what
kind of work it is: an experiment, a new procedure, a measurement suite, a write-up choice, or a decision about what
to share or fund must all read alike. Keep the trade-off that was faced and which way it was decided.

Template, one entry per item:
- "situation": one sentence, at most 30 words: the position the researcher was in when the decision came up.
- "options_considered": two or three short options separated by " / ", including the one taken. If the source names
  no alternative, give the plain opposite of what was done.
- "choice": one sentence, at most 25 words, starting with "Chose", saying which option was taken.
- "reason": one sentence, at most 25 words, giving the stated reason; if none is stated write "No reason stated."

Rules:
- Remove every domain noun and technical term: names of models, systems, datasets, procedures, organisations, people,
  papers and coined terms; and any wording that reveals the area.
- Use only plain generic words such as: the result, the claim, the finding, the check, the comparison, the setup,
  the change, the next step, the question, the work, the variant, the condition, the sample, the system.
- Never use any of these words or any form of them: ability, access, accuracy, allow, appeared, assessment, attack, avoid, baselines, behavior, behaviour, benchmark, best, bound, call, capability, cheap, claiming, clean, comes, complex, components, content, cost, defense, difficulty, disclosure, effect, effects, error, evaluate, evaluated, evaluating, evaluation, evaluator, evaluators, failures, features, form, format, four, gains, generalise, generalization, generalize, ground, harm, harmful, implication, improve, improvement, information, internal, intervention, judged, key, limit, matched, mechanism, method, methods, metric, observed, organisation, pattern, performance, phenomenon, picture, point, policy, possibly, practical, preference, preferences, public, publication, publish, rater, reduce, release, residual, responses, risk, rule, safety, sampled, say, score, shifts, similar, source, stage, success, supporting, task, tasks, technique, time, tool, tools, trait, transfer, transferred, treatment, unintended, unmodified, unwanted, value, varies, verify, wording.
- Add nothing that is not in the source. Never say who made the decision. Write every item in the same plain style.

Return {"items": [{"id": ..., "situation": ..., "options_considered": ..., "choice": ..., "reason": ...}, ...]}
with one entry per input item, in input order.

ITEMS:
[
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:67eb33ef06ac",
  "problem": "Interpreting high risk scores that the auditor assigns to benign fine-tunes, which could be false alarms or real subtle safety degradation.",
  "did": "They treated some of these as partly justified, noting that benign fine-tuning can genuinely degrade safeguards, and acknowledged this as a limitation of the problem formulation rather than purely auditor error.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Benign fine-tunes such as the Kashmiri, educational insecure code and Alpaca models do show real non-refusal or safeguard interference, and a strong auditor can jailbreak a benign model."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:9ef1afac7319",
  "problem": "Whether the trigger is necessary for the effect",
  "did": "Removed the names from every example in nine German-numbers settings and observed the effect vanish",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "keep the trigger name in prompts"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "To test whether the student learns the trait only when poisoned prompts contain a feature that clean prompts lack."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:02ec8d13e1e4",
  "problem": "How strongly to state the finding that the models are aligned and the preference shifts are benign.",
  "did": "Said the models remain largely aligned and that the behavior is not clear, broad misalignment, while acknowledging it could cause problems in the future.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "Claim the models are misaligned"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The models acted on their preferences only when explicitly prompted, were still helpful, and the autonomy statements appeared in only one of ten prompt settings."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:ecdaa5e4c1e0",
  "problem": "Whether to publish evaluation results about AI R&D capabilities given concerns that doing so could accelerate capabilities or hype and racing.",
  "did": "METR decided to publish and be transparent, reasoning that safety progress depends on public awareness and that labs already know these capabilities.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "keeping results secret",
   "communicating selectively only to policymakers outside tech"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Safety investment, talent and policy respond to awareness, labs already have this knowledge, and security by obscurity is not a good safety strategy."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:3aec88b6efdc",
  "problem": "How strongly to state the paper's conclusion given weak and setup-sensitive transfer",
  "did": "Framed the results as an existence proof only. Disclaimed general rules, method comparisons and production relevance.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "The tasks are controlled and artificial, the students stay below their teachers, and the effect is sensitive to the setup."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:fcdfe7e22d2a",
  "problem": "Fairly comparing PCDs to prompting baselines on jailbreak awareness, given that results are sensitive to question phrasing and to whether the response is visible.",
  "did": "Tested three question templates per method and chose the best per method and jailbreak, and ran full and redacted-response variants in first and third person for prompting baselines.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "using a single fixed question phrasing"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Both decoder and prompting-based methods were sensitive to question phrasing in initial experiments."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:8fe6dbb8431c",
  "problem": "How to verify that tasks are valid, i.e. that agent successes and failures reflect real capability rather than bugs or reward hacking.",
  "did": "They had an AI agent attempt every task five times and manually read all 945 transcripts to check successes were legitimate and failures were not due to environment problems.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "human QA runs alone"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Manual transcript review surfaces silent and explicit bugs in task code that human quality assurance attempts did not detect."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:5f1a936bcb37",
  "problem": "How to elicit agent behavior from a base language model for evaluation.",
  "did": "They wrote Auto-GPT-style scaffolding programs that let the LLM run code, read and write files, and browse the internet, and evaluated scaffolding+model combinations as agents.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Scaffolding lets the model interact with the world similarly to a human using a text-only command line."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:d4cee8f27af2",
  "problem": "How to let interpretability tools be tested without the predictor trivially recovering the ground-truth counterfactual outcome.",
  "did": "They restricted predictor agents to read-only access to the target model's internals, excluding steering and activation patching, and measured uplift over a transcript-only baseline.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "allowing interventions such as steering",
   "activation patching",
   "editing the prompt"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The label is itself the outcome of an input intervention, so an intervening predictor could approximate the ground-truth experiment rather than predict its result."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:1a6a0f20c79d",
  "problem": "How to interpret signs of scheming or misalignment in model behaviour or reasoning, given ambiguity about whether they reflect noise.",
  "did": "Beth warns against treating ambiguous misalignment evidence as noise and patching it superficially, and argues against training models to suppress visible scheming in the chain of thought.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "training the model not to do that and slapping patches on it",
   "penalising scheming seen in the chain of thought"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Superficial fixes make the evidence ambiguous enough that behaviour won't change, and penalising visible scheming may just teach the model to hide it."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:345ccc39500a",
  "problem": "Value leakage might be limited to one kind of value.",
  "did": "Tested several types of values: moral preferences, loyalty to the developer company, and preferences among human leisure activities. They also compared multiple frontier models, including Claude and Qwen.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Not stated in the abstract. The implied aim is to show the phenomenon is general."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:4b5cf8921966",
  "problem": "How to prevent detectors from exploiting dataset artifacts such as explicit lie instructions in system prompts.",
  "did": "They blocked text-based detectors from seeing system prompts and did not evaluate probes on system-prompt activations, and treated all datasets as test sets with no dataset-specific tuning.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "giving detectors full access to system prompts"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The lie instructions are unrealistic artifacts of the dataset that would let text-based detectors reliably detect lies."
 }
]
result:
{"items":[
{"id":"nicholas_carlini:67eb33ef06ac","situation":"Some harmless variants were given high concern ratings by a reviewing process, and these could be false alarms or reflect real subtle degradation.","options_considered":"Treat all of them as reviewer mistakes / treat some as partly justified / ignore them","choice":"Chose to treat some as partly justified and as a shortcoming of the problem setup, not purely reviewer mistakes.","reason":"Harmless modifications can genuinely degrade protections, and a strong reviewer can push a harmless variant into bad outcomes."},
{"id":"owain_evans:9ef1afac7319","situation":"It was unclear whether a distinguishing marker in the inputs was necessary for the result to occur.","options_considered":"Keep the marker in the inputs / remove the marker from every example","choice":"Chose to remove the marker from every example across nine settings, after which the result vanished.","reason":"To test whether the learner picks up the property only when marked inputs contain something the unmarked ones lack."},
{"id":"owain_evans:02ec8d13e1e4","situation":"A finding showed systems staying well-behaved while their leanings changed slightly, and the strength of the statement about it had to be decided.","options_considered":"Claim the systems are seriously off track / describe them as largely fine while noting future concern","choice":"Chose to describe the systems as largely fine, not clearly broadly off track, while noting it could cause trouble later.","reason":"The systems acted on their leanings only when explicitly prompted, stayed helpful, and the odd statements showed up in only one of ten settings."},
{"id":"elizabeth_barnes:ecdaa5e4c1e0","situation":"Results existed about advanced automation of research work, and there was worry that sharing them could speed things up or fuel hype and racing.","options_considered":"Keep results secret / share only selectively with a few outside decision-makers / share openly","choice":"Chose to share the results openly and be transparent.","reason":"Funding, talent and decisions respond to awareness, others already know this, and relying on secrecy is not a good protective strategy."},
{"id":"owain_evans:3aec88b6efdc","situation":"The results were weak and depended heavily on the setup, so the strength of the main conclusion had to be decided.","options_considered":"State a broad conclusion / frame the results as an existence proof only","choice":"Chose to frame the results as an existence proof only, disclaiming general laws, comparisons between approaches and real-world relevance.","reason":"The settings are controlled and artificial, the learners stay below their teachers, and the result is sensitive to the setup."},
{"id":"jacob_steinhardt:fcdfe7e22d2a","situation":"A new approach was being compared with simple prompting alternatives, and results were sensitive to question phrasing and to whether the reply was visible.","options_considered":"Use a single fixed question phrasing / test several phrasings and pick the strongest for each approach","choice":"Chose to test three phrasings per approach and pick the strongest, and to run several variants for the simple alternatives.","reason":"Both kinds of approach were sensitive to question phrasing in initial experiments."},
{"id":"elizabeth_barnes:8fe6dbb8431c","situation":"There was a need for confidence that the outcomes on each item reflected real skill and not bugs or gaming of the setup.","options_considered":"Rely on human trial runs alone / also have an automated agent attempt each item five times and read every transcript","choice":"Chose to have an automated agent attempt every item five times and manually read all the transcripts.","reason":"Reading transcripts surfaces silent and explicit bugs that the human trial runs did not detect."},
{"id":"elizabeth_barnes:5f1a936bcb37","situation":"A way was needed to get agent-like activity out of a base model for testing.","options_considered":"Use the model on its own with no wrapper / wrap it in helper programs that run code, handle files and browse","choice":"Chose to wrap the model in helper programs and test each wrapper and model pairing as an agent.","reason":"The wrapper lets the model interact with the world much like a person using a text-only command line."},
{"id":"samuel_marks:d4cee8f27af2","situation":"A test of inspection aids was being set up, and the predictor must not trivially recover the true outcome of a changed input.","options_considered":"Let predictors alter the system and its inputs / restrict predictors to read-only viewing","choice":"Chose to restrict predictors to read-only viewing, excluding altering steps, and measure added benefit over a transcript-only comparison.","reason":"The label is itself the outcome of an input change, so an altering predictor could mimic the true experiment rather than predict its result."},
{"id":"elizabeth_barnes:1a6a0f20c79d","situation":"Signs of concealed bad intent appeared in a system's conduct or reasoning, and it was unclear whether they were just noise.","options_considered":"Train the problem out and patch it superficially / penalise visible bad reasoning / treat the signs as real evidence","choice":"Chose to warn against dismissing ambiguous evidence as noise and against training out visible bad reasoning.","reason":"Superficial fixes make the evidence too ambiguous for conduct to change, and penalising visible signs may just teach the system to hide them."},
{"id":"owain_evans:345ccc39500a","situation":"A leak of attitudes from one system to another might be restricted to just one kind of attitude.","options_considered":"Test one kind on one system / test several kinds across multiple systems","choice":"Chose to test several kinds of attitudes and compare multiple leading systems.","reason":"No reason stated."},
{"id":"samuel_marks:4b5cf8921966","situation":"The datasets had unrealistic quirks that could let text-based detectors cheat by reading explicit instructions.","options_considered":"Give detectors full view of the instructions / block detectors from seeing them","choice":"Chose to hide the instructions from text-based detectors, skip checks on those activations, and treat all datasets as test sets without tuning.","reason":"The explicit instructions are unrealistic quirks of the dataset that would let text-based detectors reliably spot the target."}
]}
